_about: Feature-length versions (350-500 words) of the first 10 live stories. Built only from the verified fact lists in data/reel-*.json (facts + notUsed), the post texts in publish/reels/*.md and their notes. Each 'sections' entry becomes an H2 heading. Sources: 'Title | Publisher | URL' (replace the live list).

bass-reeves.excerpt: He arrested his own son. Bass Reeves wore the badge for 32 years.
sections: The deputy who could not read
Bass Reeves was born into slavery in Arkansas in 1838. During the Civil War he escaped and found refuge in Indian Territory, the land that is now Oklahoma. He never learned to read or write.

In 1875 he was commissioned as a deputy U.S. marshal for the federal court of Judge Isaac Parker at Fort Smith, Arkansas. He was one of the first Black federal lawmen west of the Mississippi River. Unable to read his warrants, he memorised them, and the writs that went with them, before he rode out.
Thirty-two years with the badge

Reeves served as a deputy U.S. marshal for 32 years. By 1901, a newspaper reported that he had arrested more than 3,000 people. That figure comes from a single newspaper report of the time, so it is best read as a contemporary estimate rather than an official count.

Popular retellings add more: that he killed fourteen outlaws, that he never arrested the wrong man, that he was the real-life model for the Lone Ranger. The first two rest on one source, or on a source that only says it "is said"; the Lone Ranger link is a theory that has never been proven. None of them is repeated here as fact.
The hardest warrant

Then came the warrant no lawman would want. His own son, Bennie, was charged with murdering his wife. Reeves took the warrant himself and brought his son in. Bennie was convicted and sent to the federal prison at Leavenworth.

Later versions of the story describe a long, dramatic manhunt. A newspaper report from 1902 says instead that Bennie surrendered. What the record supports is simpler and, in its way, harder: the father served the warrant, and the son went to prison.
After statehood
When Oklahoma became a state in 1907, Reeves's federal job ended. He was 67. He joined the police force in Muskogee, Oklahoma, and served there for about two more years.
Bass Reeves died in Muskogee on 12 January 1910. For him, the law came first, even when it was his own blood.

bessie-coleman.excerpt: American flight schools wouldn't teach her. So she learned French, sailed to France and became the first African American woman with a pilot's licence.
sections: Thirteen children, one manicurist
Bessie Coleman was born in Texas in 1892, one of thirteen children. As a young woman she moved to Chicago, where she worked as a manicurist. It was there that she decided she wanted to fly.
Flight schools in the United States turned her down, because she was Black and because she was a woman. Coleman did not give up on flying. She gave up on American flight schools instead.
Learning French to learn to fly

She learned French so that she could apply to schools in France, and in November 1920 she sailed across the Atlantic. She trained at the Caudron brothers' school at Le Crotoy, in the fragile biplanes of the day.

On 15 June 1921, the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale issued her licence. The document survives in the Smithsonian's collection. With it, Bessie Coleman became the first African American woman to hold a pilot's licence.
Queen Bess

Back in the United States, Coleman made her living as a stunt flier. She flew loops and figure eights at air shows, and the crowds gave her a name: Queen Bess. In the years of Jim Crow segregation, she pushed back against segregated audiences at her own shows.
Flying was dangerous. In 1923 she crashed in California and broke her leg. She recovered, and she flew again.
The school she never opened
Coleman was saving to open a flight school for Black pilots. On 30 April 1926, she died in a crash while rehearsing for an air show. The school was never built.

Two quotes often attributed to her, a telegram sent from her hospital bed and a line in a 1921 newspaper, each rest on a single source and are not repeated here. A claim that she was also the first Native American woman pilot is contested and is left out for the same reason.

booker-t-washington.excerpt: One dinner with the President. The South exploded.
sections: From slavery to Tuskegee

Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia in 1856. After the Civil War he fought hard for an education, and in 1881 he founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. He built it into one of the leading schools for Black Americans.
In 1896 he recruited a young scientist named George Washington Carver to lead Tuskegee's agricultural work. Carver stayed for the rest of his life.
16 October 1901

On 16 October 1901, only weeks into his presidency, Theodore Roosevelt invited Washington to dinner at the White House. That evening Booker T. Washington sat down to eat with the President and the Roosevelt family.

When the news broke, white Southern newspapers erupted. The Atlanta Constitution denounced the dinner as an insult. The Memphis Scimitar called it an outrage. A storm of fury came from white Southerners; the Theodore Roosevelt Center describes it as a firestorm.
Never invited back
Roosevelt went on consulting Washington for years afterwards. But he never invited him back to dine at the White House.

The dinner is often described as the first time a Black guest dined at the White House. The sources we checked word that claim differently, so it is not made here. Reports that some Southerners called for Roosevelt's impeachment, and that a Southern senator made threats, each appear in only one of the sources we checked, and are left out as well.
What one meal showed
Booker T. Washington died in 1915. The school he founded in 1881 still stands, and the scientist he recruited became one of the most famous in America.
One meal, and the reaction to it, showed how far the country still had to go.

ellen-craft.excerpt: In 1848, an enslaved woman escaped disguised as a white slave owner, and her husband played her slave.
sections: Macon, Georgia, 1848

Ellen and William Craft were both enslaved in Macon, Georgia. Ellen was the daughter of an enslaved woman and her white enslaver, and she looked white. In December 1848 the couple turned that fact into a plan.
Ellen would travel as a white slaveholder, a planter going north for medical treatment. William would travel as the slave who waited on him.
The disguise

Ellen cut her hair short and put on a top hat and green spectacles. She bandaged her face, as if she were an invalid, which also hid a face with no beard. She put her right arm in a sling: she could not write, and a traveller would be asked to sign his name.
There was one more problem. A planter would be expected to talk. So Ellen pretended to be hard of hearing.
A thousand miles

In December 1848 they took the train from Macon to Savannah. A friend of Ellen's enslaver sat down next to her in the carriage; her deafness kept her safe. From Savannah they went north by train and steamboat, through Charleston, Wilmington, Virginia, Washington and Baltimore.

In Baltimore an official stopped them and demanded proof that William belonged to the man he was travelling with. They were allowed to board. They reached Philadelphia on Christmas Day 1848. Sources differ on the exact day they set out, between 18 and 24 December. "A thousand miles" is the title they later gave their journey, an approximation rather than a measured distance.
Hunted again

In 1850, after the Fugitive Slave Act, two slave catchers, Hughes and Knight, came to Boston to take them back. The Crafts fled to England. There, in 1860, they published their own account, Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom.

Several details repeated elsewhere, a line Ellen is said to have spoken on arrival, a stay at the best hotel in Charleston, a first-class carriage, rest on a single source each and are not included here.

frederick-douglass.excerpt: He posed for more photos than Lincoln. On purpose.
sections: The boy who was not supposed to read

Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Talbot County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, around 1818. Like most enslaved children, he was never told his birthday; later in life he chose one for himself, 14 February. His mother, Harriet Bailey, was enslaved on a farm miles away. He remembered seeing her only a few times, always at night, after she had walked all that way to lie beside him until he slept. She died when he was about seven.

As a boy he was sent to Baltimore, to the household of Hugh and Sophia Auld. Sophia began teaching him the alphabet, until her husband found out and stopped the lessons: reading, he warned, would ruin a boy for slavery. Frederick drew the opposite conclusion. He traded bread to hungry white boys in the street in exchange for reading lessons, and at about twelve he got hold of a book of speeches, The Columbian Orator.
The fight, and the escape

As a teenager he was hired out to Edward Covey, a farmer known for breaking the will of enslaved people. After months of beatings, the sixteen-year-old fought back, in a struggle he later said lasted nearly two hours. He stayed enslaved for four more years, but wrote that he was never really whipped again.

On 3 September 1838 he escaped, travelling north by train and steamboat dressed as a sailor and carrying the papers of a free Black seaman. He reached New York the next day. Anna Murray, a free Black woman who had helped plan the escape, joined him, and they married within days. They settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where their host suggested a new last name from Walter Scott’s poem The Lady of the Lake. From then on he was Frederick Douglass.
A voice the country could not ignore

In August 1841 he spoke at an anti-slavery meeting on Nantucket and soon became one of the leading abolitionist speakers of his time. In 1845 he published the Narrative of his life, naming names, places and dates. That made him easy to find, so he spent almost two years speaking in Britain and Ireland, where friends raised £150 and bought his freedom from Hugh Auld in December 1846.

In 1847 he founded his own newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester, New York. The next year he attended the first women’s rights convention at Seneca Falls, and on 5 July 1852 he gave one of the most famous speeches in American history, asking what the Fourth of July meant to the enslaved.
Fighting with a camera

In Douglass’s time, most images of Black Americans were demeaning: cartoons drawn to mock. Douglass answered with the newest technology of the age. From his earliest known photograph in 1841 to his death, he sat for his portrait whenever he could: serious, dignified, looking straight at the camera. Historians who set out to collect every photograph of him found more than 160 separate portraits, more than Abraham Lincoln. The count comes from the research behind the 2015 book Picturing Frederick Douglass and is repeated by the National Park Service.

He also lectured on pictures, including a talk called Pictures and Progress, about the power of images to change how people see one another. It is often said he never smiled for the camera; one source says he almost never did, so the stronger claim is not made here.
Lincoln, and Cedar Hill

During the Civil War, Douglass recruited Black soldiers for the Union; two of his sons served. In August 1863 he went to the White House, uninvited, to protest the lower pay and worse treatment of Black soldiers, and met Lincoln face to face. On the night of Lincoln’s second inauguration, in March 1865, police stopped him at the door; Lincoln had him let in.

After the war Douglass served as U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia and later as minister to Haiti. He died at Cedar Hill, his home in Washington, on 20 February 1895, after a day spent at a meeting of the National Council of Women.

garrett-morgan.excerpt: He walked into deadly gas. On purpose. Then the news reports left him out.
sections: The hood
Garrett A. Morgan was a Black inventor in Cleveland, Ohio, born in 1877. In 1914 he patented a breathing device, a safety hood that let the wearer breathe in smoke and gas.
Racism hurt his sales. To sell the hood, he hired a white man, and at times white actors, to present it.
24 July 1916
On 24 July 1916 an explosion hit a waterworks tunnel being dug under Lake Erie, and gas filled the tunnel. Workers were trapped. Men who went in to rescue them were overcome by the gas and died.

The Cleveland police called Morgan. He and his brother Frank, with others, went into the tunnel wearing the hoods, and they brought out survivors. Sources disagree on how many: the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History records two rescued and four bodies recovered, while the Patent Office and Britannica say eight survivors. No number is claimed here.
Left out of the story
Other rescuers were rewarded. Morgan was denied the money they received, and his part in the rescue was left out of national news reports.

A popular account says he had earlier disguised himself as a Native American assistant to sell his invention. Among the sources we checked, only the Patent Office tells that story, so it is not repeated here.
The traffic signal

Years later, after witnessing a collision at an intersection, Morgan patented a traffic signal: US patent 1,475,024, granted on 20 November 1923. General Electric bought the rights for 40,000 dollars.
He is often credited with inventing the traffic light. He did not. He patented an improved three-position signal, with a warning position between stop and go. Garrett Morgan died in 1963.

george-washington-carver.excerpt: As a baby, he was traded for a horse. He grew up to be one of the most famous scientists in America.
sections: Kidnapped

George Washington Carver was born into slavery on Moses Carver’s farm near Diamond, Missouri, near the end of the Civil War. No one wrote down the date; even the year is uncertain, probably around 1864. While he was still a baby, raiders carried him and his mother, Mary, away from the farm. Moses Carver sent someone after them. The baby was found and brought back, and getting him back cost Moses Carver a horse; one early biography says a racehorse. Accounts differ on who searched and exactly what was paid. His mother was never found.
A boy who loved plants

After slavery ended, Moses and Susan Carver raised George and his older brother Jim. George was small and often ill, so he stayed near the house and the garden, and fell in love with plants. No school nearby would take a Black child; Susan Carver taught him to read and write. While still a boy he walked about eight miles to Neosho, the nearest town with a school for Black children, where he lodged with Andrew and Mariah Watkins.

Highland College in Kansas accepted him by letter, then turned him away when he arrived and they saw he was Black. He studied art at Simpson College in Iowa, where his teacher Etta Budd noticed how much he knew about plants and sent him to Iowa State. In 1893 his painting Yucca and Cactus received an honourable mention at the Chicago World’s Fair.
Iowa State, then Tuskegee

At Iowa State, Carver was the first Black student. He earned a bachelor’s degree in agriculture in 1894, stayed for graduate work on plant diseases, earned a master’s in 1896 and became the school’s first Black faculty member. That year a letter came from Booker T. Washington, asking him to lead the agriculture work at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Carver said yes and stayed nearly fifty years.

There was almost no laboratory, so Carver and his students built their equipment from bottles, jars and scrap found in trash heaps. In the South, many Black farmers were trapped growing cotton on worn-out land. Carver urged them to rotate crops and plant peanuts and sweet potatoes, wrote plain bulletins with advice and recipes, and sent a farm school on wheels, the Jesup Wagon, to those who could not come to him. When the boll weevil destroyed cotton crops in the early 1900s, his message mattered more than ever.
Ten minutes in Congress

In January 1921 Carver testified before the House Ways and Means Committee for the peanut growers. He was given ten minutes. He unpacked his samples, and the congressmen kept extending his time. After that he was famous across the country, and in 1923 the NAACP awarded him its Spingarn Medal.

With fame came myths. Carver did not invent peanut butter; peanut pastes existed before his work. The claim that he found 300 uses for the peanut is contested: many of the items were ideas or recipes, and he held only three patents in his life. He did not want to get rich. He wanted poor farmers to survive.
A monument

Carver died at Tuskegee on 5 January 1943. Months later, in July 1943, the Missouri farm where he was born became the George Washington Carver National Monument, the first national monument to honour an African American.

harriet-tubman.excerpt: In 1863, a woman led a military raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people in one night.
sections: Before the war

Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland around 1820. She escaped in 1849, and then went back, again and again, to guide others out. Over about ten years on the Underground Railroad she led roughly 70 people to freedom.
In one night in 1863 she would help free ten times that number.
Scout and spy

During the Civil War, Tubman served the Union in South Carolina as a scout and spy. She recruited scouts who gathered intelligence on the Combahee River area, including the positions of Confederate mines, called torpedoes at the time, in the river.
The night of 1 June 1863

On the night of 1 June 1863, Tubman guided three Union gunboats, the John Adams, the Harriet A. Weed and the Sentinel, up the Combahee River, alongside Colonel James Montgomery. About 300 soldiers took part: the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers, a Black regiment, with about 50 men from a Rhode Island unit.

As the gunboats came up the river, enslaved people ran and swam towards them. Plantations, rice mills and supplies along the river were burned. By the morning of 2 June, more than 700 people were free. Sources give the exact count as 727, 750 or 756; "more than 700" is the figure they agree on. Many of the freed men enlisted in the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers.
Who led the raid

Tubman is often called the first woman in American history to lead a military raid. The US House of Representatives' history office puts it more precisely: she was the first African American woman to lead troops in a military operation, and she guided the raid with Colonel Montgomery. That is the claim made here.

She was never paid a soldier's pension for her service. She received a widow's pension, as the widow of Nelson Davis, from 1892; it was raised to 20 dollars a month in 1899. Harriet Tubman died in 1913.

henry-box-brown.excerpt: He mailed himself to freedom: 27 hours in a wooden box, part of it upside down.
sections: Richmond, 1848

Henry Brown was born into slavery in Virginia around 1815 or 1816. He worked in a tobacco factory in Richmond. In 1848 his wife, Nancy, and their three children were sold to an owner in North Carolina.
The next year, he decided to leave Virginia in a way no one would expect.
This side up with care

On 23 March 1849, two helpers, James C. A. Smith and Samuel A. Smith, sealed Brown into a wooden box about three feet long, two feet wide and two and a half feet deep. It was marked "This side up with care". The 1849 narrative's own drawing of the box reads "Right side up with care"; William Still's 1872 account and Brown's later narrative give the first wording.

The box was handed to a private express company and travelled by wagon, railroad and steamboat to Philadelphia. The label did not help much. At one point the box was turned upside down, and Brown rode on his head for a long stretch. He stayed still and silent the whole way. The journey took 26 or 27 hours, depending on the source.
Philadelphia

At the Anti-Slavery office in Philadelphia, abolitionists including James Miller McKim opened the box. Brown climbed out alive and sang a hymn based on Psalm 40. From then on he was Henry "Box" Brown.

A greeting he is said to have offered on climbing out appears only in Still's account, so it is not quoted here. The distance he travelled is sometimes given as 350 miles, a figure found only on popular sites.
England
After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, Brown feared capture. In October 1850 he sailed to England, where he toured with a moving panorama and stage shows. He died in 1897.
Whether he ever saw his wife and children again is often stated with certainty. The sources we checked do not settle it, so no claim is made here.

hiram-revels.excerpt: Mississippi sent America's first Black senator. In 1870.
sections: Born free

Hiram Rhodes Revels was born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on 27 September 1827. He studied at seminaries in Indiana and Ohio and later at Knox College in Illinois. He was ordained a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and he preached and taught across the Midwest and the South.

During the Civil War he helped recruit Black regiments for the Union and served as chaplain to a Black regiment in Mississippi. After the war he settled in Natchez, Mississippi, and in 1869 he was elected to the state senate.
Chosen by the legislature

At the time, state legislatures chose U.S. senators, not voters. In January 1861, Mississippi’s senator Jefferson Davis had walked out of the Senate to lead the Confederacy. Nine years later, on 20 January 1870, Mississippi’s new legislature voted 85 to 15 to send Hiram Revels to Washington.
Forty-eight to eight

Senate Democrats tried to stop him. They argued that a Black man could not have been a citizen for the nine years the Constitution requires of a senator, and they pointed to the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision to say so.
On 25 February 1870, the Senate voted 48 to 8 to seat him. Hiram Revels became the first African American to serve in the United States Congress.
Whose seat it was
It is often said that Revels took Jefferson Davis's old seat. He did not. He filled the seat once held by Albert G. Brown; Davis's former seat went to Adelbert Ames.

In his year in the Senate, Revels spoke up for Black legislators who had been expelled in Georgia and opposed keeping Washington’s schools segregated. After his term he became the first president of Alcorn University in Mississippi, in 1871. He died in 1901.
